Miller said trucking companies will absorb some of the extra costs from the tolls, but they will have to pass on a portion of the fees to customers such as restaurants and bars that already operate on thin margins.
Freight companies and their customers say the charges will pile on costs for cargo that can’t reach its destination any other way.

Continued from page B1
“A restaurant’s fish order is not taking the subway from the Bronx to Midtown Manhattan,” said Andrew Rigie, executive director of New York City Hospitality Alliance, which represents restaurants, bars and nightclubs.
“That truck has to come into the zone and our suppliers have told us this is going to increase their cost of doing business,” Rigie said.
About 120,000 trucks and commercial vehicles enter the city each day, according to the city transportation department.
GUERIN CHARLES/ABACA/ZUMA PRESS

John Luciani, an executive at A. Duie Pyle, a West Chester, Pa.-based trucking company focused on the Northeast that consolidates shipments from multiple customers in a single trailer, says New York City is already the most difficult and expensive city it operates in.

Luciani said that because of traffic, A. Duie Pyle’s drivers there average eight deliveries and pickups a day, compared with an average of 23 daily deliveries and pickups across the wider region. He said average toll costs per delivery are almost three times higher in the city than regionwide.
“The cost of doing business in NYC is significant,” he said.
City and state transportation officials say truckers can reduce costs by delivering overnight. The congestion toll for heavy-duty trucks drops to $5.40 during off-peak hours.
Carriers say they already have plenty of incentives to deliver overnight.
Traffic is lighter and curb space is available. But they say many customers can’t accept overnight deliveries because they don’t have overnight staff or a secure location for unattended deliveries.
“It’s just another tax and another cost of doing business in the Big Apple,” Luciani said.

Law Firms
Prepare for
Trump
Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said his company wouldn’t work with any firm that hires certain Biden-era regulators.

Continued from page B1
trade adviser

Top firms across the U.S. are also bracing for major changes in the antitrust landscape. President Biden appointed officials, including Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan, who sought to increase enforcement to levels not seen in decades. That created a lucrative environment for antitrust lawyers as companies struggled to secure government clearance for a range of proposed mergers and acquisitions.

Trump’s new administration likely means a more hands-off approach, which in some ways could reduce the windfall for antitrust litigators and counselors. But the more predictable and favorable regulatory climate, along with economic factors, could drive new corporate dealmaking and provide a healthy stream of legal revenue.

Ropes & Gray antitrust partner Jonathan Klarfeld said he expects his practice area to return to a normal baseline after years of drawn-out enforcement built on progressive and untested legal theories.
“Some of the excesses of recent enforcement are likely to be pared back,” Klarfeld said, but added, “There is more than enough work to occupy our time.”
The charged political environment is spurring specialty practice areas designed to help clients navigate it.

Labor-law specialist firm Seyfarth Shaw created a cultural-flashpoints task force in 2023 to help clients navigate workplace challenges and respond to rising pressure for companies to take a stance on social issues, said Lorie Almon, the firm’s chair and managing partner.

The firm is now marketing the practice anew after the divisiveness of the 2024 election and a backlash against some policies embraced by progressives. The group helps employers “lower the temperature” around hot-button social and political issues, Almon said.

More broadly, law firms are beginning to be more hesitant about taking public stances that could anger Trump and his allies, after years in which firms weren't shy about speaking out on issues including abortion rights, racial justice and the war in the Middle East.
“They are more sensitive to this now than they have been in the past,” said law firm consultant Peter Zeughauser. “They are more careful.”

Four years ago, some firms sought to distance themselves from Trump after he sought to overturn Joe Biden’s 2020 electoral victory. The positioning across the industry is far different now, and former Trump officials have become highly prized assets.
“Firms are peacocking their Trump feathers in a way we haven’t seen in recent memory,” said Dan Binstock, a legal recruiter based in Washington.

Among the firms eager to champion its D.C. ties is Akin, which has been pitching itself as particularly well placed for the coming administration. Its marketing tools include a new biweekly policy publication on how clients can navigate the postelection landscape.

The firm’s roster of D.C. insiders includes former Rep. Kevin Brady, who as Republican chair of the House Ways and Means Committee during the first Trump administration helped usher in a sweeping package of tax cuts—many of which are set to expire at the end of this year.
“We have a pulse on all things Washington,” said Abid Qureshi, Akin’s co-chair-elect.

Even before the election, top firms were engaged in a poaching war for star partners with expertise that could bring in new portfolios of business. Trump’s victory—and the policy upheavals that come with it—only adds to that pressure.
“If law firms haven’t invested in the regulatory space, it may be too late to recruit top talent,” said Yvette Ostolaza, chair of Sidley Austin’s management committee.

Much of Anthropic’s funding to date has come from its close partner Amazon.com, which committed $4 billion to the startup in November, bringing its total investment since 2023 to $8 billion. Amazon’s November investment was a convertible note, meaning it will translate to equity at the valuation set in the current round.

Anthropic develops and operates its technology in data centers operated by Amazon and Google, which also has invested billions of dollars in the startup. GFL Environmental to
Sell Services Business
In $5.6 Billion Deal
BY DENNY JACOB

GFL Environmental has reached an agreement to sell its environmental services business in a deal valued at 8 billion Canadian dollars, equivalent to about $5.59 billion, though it would retain an equity interest.

The Canadian company, which transports and recycles waste, among other services, said it reached the agreement with funds managed by affiliates of Apollo and BC Partners. It would retain a 44% equity interest in the business, while funds managed by affiliates of Apollo and BC each would hold a 28% equity interest.
GFL said its board, when excluding interested directors who have recused themselves, has unanimously approved the transaction. The deal is expected to close in the first quarter.

GFL expects cash proceeds from the deal to be around C$6.2 billion. It intends to use up to C$3.75 billion of the net proceeds to repay debt, leaving up to C$2.25 billion for share repurchases. The balance will go to transaction fees and general corporate purposes.

Chief Executive Patrick Dovigi said a deleveraged balance sheet will provide GFL with more financial flexibility to deploy capital into organic growth initiatives and solid waste M&A and allow for a greater return of capital to shareholders.
Dovigi said the company will maintain an option to repurchase the environmental services business within five years of closing.
CHARD B. LEVINE/LEVINE ROBERTS/NEWSCOM/ZUMA PRESS
The latest proposal from Cintas, a maker of workplace products, was initially given to UniFirst's board in November.

Cintas Bids
For Rival
UniFirst

Continued from page B1
engage with UniFirst, including by stating its willingness to consider increasing its offer price, a subsequent letter says.
UniFirst has told Cintas that its board unanimously concluded that a deal wasn’t in the best interest of the company and its stakeholders, according to correspondence in December and November.
In October, UniFirst had said in a news release that it was excited about the investments it was making and believed its business had “significant long-term potential.”
For Cintas, a deal would allow the combined companies to serve more customers and make greater use of its recent investments in technology and infrastructure.

Cintas also thinks investors would like the deal: 79% of UniFirst common shares are held by investors who also own Cintas’s stock, according to a Cintas analysis included in the letters delivered to UniFirst’s board.
A deal for UniFirst, should it happen, would be Cintas’s biggest transaction yet.
Cintas is led by Chief Executive Officer Todd Schneider, who has held that role since June 2021.
